An FRN pays **MRR + quoted margin (QM)**, where QM is fixed at issue to compensate for the issuer's credit risk at that time.

The **discount margin (DM)** (required margin) is the spread investors require *today*.

- DM = QM → FRN priced at par on reset dates
- DM > QM (credit worsened) → **discount**
- DM < QM (credit improved) → **premium**

This mirrors coupon vs YTM for fixed-rate bonds.

cards.title: FRN pricing model
cards.formula: PV = Σ [(MRR + QM) × FV ÷ m] ÷ [1 + (MRR + DM) ÷ m]^{t} + FV ÷ [1 + (MRR + DM) ÷ m]^{N}
cards.note: Coupon uses QM; discount rate uses DM.

cards.title: Pricing an FRN
cards.body:
3-year FRN, quarterly, MRR 4.00%, QM 0.60%, DM 0.80%.

Coupon per quarter = (4.60%/4) × 100 = 1.15
Discount rate per quarter = 4.80%/4 = 1.20%
N = 12

PV = **99.44** (discount, because DM > QM).

cards.title: Solving for the discount margin
cards.body:
2-year FRN, semiannual, MRR 3.00%, QM 0.50%, price 99.50.

Coupon = 3.50%/2 × 100 = 1.75; N = 4. Solve for the periodic rate: 1.8810%.

Annual rate = 3.762%. DM = 3.762% − 3.00% = **0.76%** (76 bp).

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Do not swap QM and DM. The **QM goes in the coupon** (PMT); the **DM goes in the discount rate** (I/Y). Swapping them in the 3-year example gives 100.56 instead of 99.44.

cards.title: Two quoting conventions
cards.body:
Money-market instruments (T-bills, CP, CDs, repos) are quoted with simple (non-compounded) rates, but in two ways:
- **Discount basis:** rate is a % of **face value** (T-bills, US CP, banker's acceptances). Understates the true return.
- **Add-on basis:** interest is added to the principal; rate is a % of **price** (CDs, repos, interbank deposits, ECP).

Year length may be **360** or **365** days depending on the market.

cards.title: Money-market formulas
cards.formula:
Discount: PV = FV × (1 − Days/Year × DR); DR = (Year/Days) × (FV − PV) ÷ FV
Add-on: PV = FV ÷ (1 + Days/Year × AOR); AOR = (Year/Days) × (FV − PV) ÷ PV
cards.note: Bond-equivalent yield (BEY) = add-on rate on a 365-day year.

cards.title: Converting a T-bill quote
cards.body:
A 180-day T-bill is quoted at a 4.00% discount rate (360-day year).

PV = 100 × (1 − 180/360 × 0.04) = **98.00**
AOR (360) = (360/180) × 2/98 = **4.08%**
BEY (365) = (365/180) × 2/98 = **4.14%**

The discount rate always looks lower than the true return because it divides by face value, not price.

cards.title: Comparing CP and a CD
cards.body:
90-day CP at a 3.90% discount rate vs a 90-day CD at a 3.95% add-on rate, both on 360 days.

CP price = 100 × (1 − 90/360 × 0.039) = 99.025
CP add-on = (360/90) × 0.975/99.025 = **3.94%**

The CD pays more (3.95% > 3.94%), although the gap is far smaller than the quotes suggest.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: To compare money-market instruments, convert everything to the **same basis**: add-on, same year length (usually 365, the BEY). Discount-basis rates are always below the equivalent add-on rate.

questions.stem: An FRN pays MRR + 0.60% quarterly and has 3 years to maturity. MRR is 4.00% and the discount margin is 0.80%. Its price per 100 par is closest to:
questions.explanation: Coupon = 4.60%/4 = 1.15; discount rate = 4.80%/4 = 1.20%; N = 12 → PV = 99.44. 100.56 swaps QM and DM; 100.00 would require DM = QM.

questions.stem: A 2-year FRN pays MRR + 0.50% semiannually. MRR is 3.00% and the FRN trades at 99.50. The discount margin is closest to:
questions.explanation: N = 4, PMT = 1.75, PV = −99.50, FV = 100 → periodic rate 1.881%, annual 3.762%. DM = 3.762% − 3.00% = 76 bp. 50 bp is the quoted margin, which applies only at par; 26 bp moves in the wrong direction (a price below par requires DM > QM).

questions.stem: Since issue, an FRN issuer's credit quality has improved. On a reset date, the FRN will most likely trade:
options: at a premium, because the discount margin is now below the quoted margin.
at a discount, because the discount margin is now above the quoted margin.
at par, because the coupon resets to market rates.
questions.explanation: Better credit lowers the required margin (DM) below the fixed QM, so the FRN pays more than investors now require and trades above par. The reset adjusts MRR but not the margin, so par holds only if DM = QM.

questions.stem: In the FRN pricing model, the quoted margin is used to determine:
questions.explanation: Coupon = (MRR + QM) × FV/m. The discount rate uses MRR + DM. The MRR itself is set by the market, not by the margin.

questions.stem: A 180-day T-bill is quoted at a 4.00% discount rate (360-day year). Its price per 100 face is closest to:
A 120-day T-bill trades at 98.75 per 100 face. Its bond-equivalent yield is closest to:
An investor compares 90-day CP quoted at a 3.90% discount rate with a 90-day CD quoted at a 3.95% add-on rate, both on a 360-day year. Which statement is most accurate?
options: The CP offers the higher return: 3.96% vs 3.95%.
The CD offers the higher return: 3.95% vs 3.94% for the CP.
Both offer the same return once converted.
questions.explanation: CP price = 99.025; add-on equivalent = (360/90) × 0.975/99.025 = 3.94%, below the CD's 3.95%. Converting a discount rate always raises it, but here not by enough to beat the CD.

questions.stem: Which money-market instrument is typically quoted on a discount basis?
questions.explanation: T-bills (and US CP, banker's acceptances) use the discount basis. CDs and repos use add-on rates.

questions.stem: A bank deposit of 1,000,000 for 90 days pays an add-on rate of 4.20% on a 365-day basis. The amount repaid at maturity is closest to:
A 180-day T-bill has a 4.00% discount rate (360-day). Its bond-equivalent yield is closest to:
questions.explanation: Price = 98.00. BEY = (365/180) × 2/98 = 4.14%. 4.08% is the add-on rate on 360 days; 4.06% applies 365/360 to the discount rate (4.00% × 365/360) without converting to an add-on basis.

questions.stem: If an FRN's discount margin rises after issue while MRR is unchanged, the FRN's price will most likely:
options: remain at par because the coupon resets.
questions.explanation: A higher DM raises the discount rate while the coupon (MRR + fixed QM) does not change, so price falls below par. Resets only adjust for MRR, not the margin.

questions.stem: Compared with the add-on rate for the same money-market instrument and year convention, the discount rate is:
questions.explanation: The discount rate divides interest by face value, which exceeds price, so it is always lower than the add-on rate.

questions.stem: A 3-year quarterly FRN with QM 0.60% trades at 99.44 when MRR is 4.00%. If the issuer is upgraded and the DM falls to 0.60%, the price on the next reset date is closest to:
questions.explanation: With DM equal to QM, the coupon rate equals the discount rate, so the FRN prices at par on a reset date. 99.44 is the old price (DM 0.80%); 100.56 would require DM below QM (e.g. 0.40%).

flashcards.back: QM is fixed in the coupon; DM is the margin required now. DM > QM → discount; DM < QM → premium.
PV = FV × (1 − Days/Year × DR)
AOR = (Year/Days) × (FV − PV) ÷ PV
Add-on rate on a 365-day year.
Discount: T-bills, US CP, BAs. Add-on: CDs, repos, deposits, ECP.
Discount rate is always lower (divides by face value, not price).

modules.title: The Term Structure of Interest Rates: Spot, Par, and Forward Curves
modules.summary: The three ways to describe the yield curve (spot, par and forward rates), how to price bonds with spot or forward rates, and how to move between the curves (bootstrapping and forward-rate calculations).

acca.note: If you took AFM, you used spot-rate yield curves (and maybe bootstrapping) to value bonds. New for CFA: par curves, implied forward rates and their notation (e.g. 2y1y), pricing with forwards, and comparing the shapes of the three curves.

lessons.title: Spot rates and pricing with spot rates

cards.title: Spot rates
cards.body:
A **spot rate** (zero rate) z_{t} is the yield on a zero-coupon bond maturing at time t. The plot of spot rates against maturity is the **spot curve**.

A coupon bond is a bundle of zeros, so each cash flow should be discounted at the spot rate for its own date, not a single YTM. If the curve is not flat, the bond's YTM is a weighted average of the spot rates.

cards.title: Spot-rate pricing
cards.body:
Spot rates: z_{1} = 3%, z_{2} = 4%, z_{3} = 5%.
Discount factors: 0.97087, 0.92456, 0.86384.

3-year 5% annual bond:
P = 5 × 0.97087 + 5 × 0.92456 + 105 × 0.86384 = **100.18**

Its YTM (about 4.93%) sits between the spot rates, closest to z_{3} because most value is in the final payment.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: AFM's 'yield curve' bond valuation is exactly spot-rate pricing. CFA adds discount-factor notation, par and forward curves, and the idea that arbitrage forces every bond to price off the same spot curve. If you skipped AFM, this is new but quick.

cards.title: Par rates
cards.body:
A **par rate** is the coupon rate that would make a bond priced off the spot curve trade exactly at par. The **par curve** is what governments' newly issued bonds approximately show.

For each maturity N, the par rate p solves:

**1 = p × (DF_{1} + … + DF_{N}) + DF_{N}**

so p = (1 − DF_{N}) ÷ Σ DF_{t}.

cards.title: Bootstrapping spot rates
cards.body:
**Bootstrapping** reverses the process: start from par rates and solve for spot rates one maturity at a time.

1. The 1-year par rate is the 1-year spot rate.
2. For year 2: 100 = p_{2} × 100 × DF_{1} + (100 + p_{2} × 100) × DF_{2}. Solve for DF_{2}, then z_{2}.
3. Repeat for each later year, using the DFs already found.

cards.title: Exam tip
cards.body: Curve ordering when the spot curve slopes **up**: forward > spot > par. When it slopes **down**: forward < spot < par. When flat, all three are equal.

cards.title: What a forward rate is
cards.body:
An **implied forward rate** is the rate for a loan starting in the future, locked in today, that is consistent with current spot rates.

Notation: **AyBy** = a B-year rate starting A years from now. **2y1y** = the 1-year rate two years forward.

Intuition: investing for 3 years at z_{3} must give the same result as investing for 2 years at z_{2} and then for 1 year at the 2y1y rate. Otherwise there is an arbitrage.

cards.title: Forward rates from spot rates
where: spot rates for A and B years (B > A)
implied forward rate for B − A years starting at A
cards.note: Quick approximation: IFR ≈ (B × z_{B} − A × z_{A}) ÷ (B − A).

cards.title: Using forward rates
cards.body:
A forward rate is a **breakeven** rate: if the future spot rate turns out equal to today's forward, returns from rolling short bonds and buying long bonds are the same.

If an investor expects future spot rates to be **below** current forward rates, longer bonds are attractive (their value will rise more than the forwards imply). This is the basis of **riding the yield curve** in an upward-sloping curve.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Use **geometric** linking, not arithmetic averaging. The approximation (B × z_{B} − A × z_{A})/(B − A) is close but slightly off: for 2y1y it gives 7.00% vs the exact 7.03%. On the exam, compute exactly unless options are far apart.

questions.stem: Spot rates are 3% (1-year), 4% (2-year) and 5% (3-year). The price of a 3-year, 5% annual-coupon bond per 100 par is closest to:
questions.explanation: P = 5/1.03 + 5/1.04^{2} + 105/1.05^{3} = 4.854 + 4.623 + 90.703 = 100.18. 100.00 discounts everything at 5% (the 3-year spot); 97.33 discounts every flow at a flat 6%, which overstates discounting.

questions.stem: Using spot rates of 3%, 4% and 5% for years 1 to 3, the price of a 3-year 6% annual bond is closest to:
questions.explanation: P = 6 × 0.97087 + 6 × 0.92456 + 106 × 0.86384 = 102.94. 100.00 assumes the 6% coupon equals the yield; 102.72 discounts every flow at the 5% 3-year spot rate.

questions.stem: The 2-year discount factor when the 2-year spot rate is 4% is closest to:
questions.explanation: DF_{2} = 1/1.04^{2} = 0.9246. 0.9259 uses simple interest (1/1.08); 0.9615 is the one-year factor 1/1.04.

questions.stem: Spot rates are 3% (1-year) and 4% (2-year). The 2-year par rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: Par = (1 − DF_{2}) ÷ (DF_{1} + DF_{2}) = (1 − 0.92456) ÷ (0.97087 + 0.92456) = 3.98%. 3.50% is the simple average of the spots; 4.00% is the 2-year spot itself. With an upward-sloping curve, par is just below the spot.

questions.stem: Par rates are 2.0% (1-year) and 3.0% (2-year), annual coupons. The bootstrapped 2-year spot rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: DF_{1} = 1/1.02 = 0.98039. 100 = 3 × 0.98039 + 103 × DF_{2} → DF_{2} = 0.94233 → z_{2} = 0.94233^{−1/2} − 1 = 3.015%. 3.000% treats par and spot as equal; 2.985% errs in the wrong direction (spot exceeds par when the curve slopes up).

questions.stem: When the spot curve is upward sloping, which ordering is correct for a given maturity beyond one year?
options: Par rate < spot rate < forward rate
Forward rate < spot rate < par rate
Spot rate < par rate < forward rate
questions.explanation: In an upward-sloping curve forwards are above spots, and par rates (weighted averages of spots that put weight on earlier, lower rates) are below spots. Forward < spot < par applies to a downward-sloping curve.

questions.stem: The 2-year spot rate is 4% and the 3-year spot rate is 5%. The 2y1y implied forward rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: 1.05^{3}/1.04^{2} − 1 = 7.03%. 7.00% is the arithmetic approximation (3 × 5 − 2 × 4); 4.50% simply averages the two spot rates.

questions.stem: The 1-year spot rate is 2.5% and the 1y1y forward rate is 3.5%. The 2-year spot rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: (1 + z_{2})^{2} = 1.025 × 1.035 → z_{2} = 2.999% ≈ 3.00%. 3.50% is the forward itself; 6.09% is the 2-year cumulative return, not an annual rate.

questions.stem: Spot rates are 3.2% (2-year) and 4.0% (5-year). The 2y3y implied forward rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: (1.04^{5}/1.032^{2})^{1/3} − 1 = 4.54%. 3.60% simply averages the two spot rates; 4.80% adds the spot difference (0.80%) to the 5-year spot. The arithmetic approximation (5 × 4.0 − 2 × 3.2)/3 = 4.53% is close to the exact geometric answer.

questions.stem: An investor expects future 1-year rates to be lower than the current implied forward rates. To maximise return, she should most likely:
questions.explanation: If future spot rates come in below today's forwards, long bonds gain more than the forwards price in, so longer bonds outperform rolling short ones. Rolling short bonds locks in the lower future rates she expects.

questions.stem: Spot rates are 3% (1-year), 4% (2-year) and 5% (3-year). The 1y2y implied forward rate is closest to:
questions.explanation: (1.05^{3}/1.03)^{1/2} − 1 = 6.01%. 5.01% is 1y1y and 7.03% is 2y1y; the 1y2y rate is roughly their geometric average.

questions.stem: Par rates are 2.0%, 3.0% and 3.5% for years 1 to 3. Given z_{1} = 2.000% and z_{2} = 3.015%, the bootstrapped 3-year spot rate is closest to:
Which statement about pricing an option-free bond is most accurate?
options: Pricing with spot rates and pricing with the corresponding forward rates give the same value.
Pricing with forward rates always gives a higher value in an upward-sloping curve.
Only YTM pricing is free of arbitrage.
questions.explanation: Forward rates are derived from spot rates, so discounting by successive forwards reproduces each spot discount factor and the same price. Arbitrage-free pricing uses spot (or forward) rates, not a single YTM.

questions.stem: With spot rates of 3%, 4% and 5%, a 3-year 5% annual bond trades at 100.18. Its YTM is closest to:
questions.explanation: Solve 100.18 = Σ 5/(1 + y)^{t} + 100/(1 + y)^{3}: y ≈ 4.93%. It is close to the 3-year spot because most of the value is the final payment, but below it because coupons are discounted at lower rates. 4.00% is the 2-year spot; 5.00% is the 3-year spot.

flashcards.back: Yield on a zero-coupon bond for maturity t; discount each cash flow at its own spot rate.
1 = p × Σ DF_{t} + DF_{N} → p = (1 − DF_{N}) ÷ Σ DF_{t}
1-year rate starting 2 years from now.
Forward > spot > par. Reverse when downward sloping.
Solve spot rates sequentially from par rates, using earlier discount factors.

modules.title: Interest Rate Risk and Return
modules.summary: Where a bond investor's return comes from (coupons, reinvestment income, price changes), how the investment horizon decides whether rising rates help or hurt, and Macaulay duration as the horizon at which those effects offset.

acca.note: AFM introduced Macaulay duration as a weighted-average time to cash flows. New for CFA: decomposing horizon returns, carrying value vs price, reinvestment vs market price risk, and the duration gap.

cards.title: Three sources of return
cards.body:
A fixed-rate bond investor earns:
1. **Coupon payments**
2. **Reinvestment income** (interest on interest) on those coupons
3. **Capital gain or loss** if sold before maturity

If the bond is held to maturity and rates never change, the realized return = the YTM at purchase. That requires every coupon to be reinvested at that same YTM.

cards.title: Two opposing rate risks
cards.body:
When yields rise:
- **Reinvestment income rises** (good)
- **Market price falls** (bad, if sold before maturity)

When yields fall, the reverse.

**Long horizon** → reinvestment effect dominates: rising rates help.
**Short horizon** → price effect dominates: rising rates hurt.

The two risks offset at a horizon equal to the bond's **Macaulay duration**.

cards.title: Horizon matters
cards.body:
Buy a 5-year 6% annual bond at par (YTM 6%). Yields immediately rise to 7% and stay there.

**Hold 5 years:** coupons reinvested at 7% grow to 34.50; plus 100 par = 134.50. Return = (134.50/100)^{1/5} − 1 = **6.11%** (> 6%).

**Sell after 2 years:** coupons with reinvestment = 12.42; sale price (3 years left, at 7%) = 97.38; total 109.80. Return = **4.78%** (< 6%).

cards.title: Carrying value and capital gains
cards.body:
A capital gain is measured against the bond's **carrying value** (the price on its constant-yield path at the purchase YTM), not the purchase price.

Example: buy the 5-year 6% bond at 95.90 (YTM 7%). After 2 years, carrying value = PV at 7% with 3 years left = 97.38. The 1.48 rise is **interest income** (amortized discount). Sell at 98.50 → capital gain = 98.50 − 97.38 = **1.12**.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Interest income for a discount bond includes the amortization of the discount, not just coupons. Only the price change **relative to carrying value** counts as a capital gain or loss.

lessons.title: Macaulay duration and the duration gap

cards.title: Macaulay duration
cards.formula: MacDur = Σ t × w_{t}, where w_{t} = PV(CF_{t}) ÷ Price
where: share of the bond's value received at time t
cards.note: Divide by periods per year to express in years. Between coupon dates, subtract t/T.

cards.title: Computing MacDur
cards.body:
3-year 6% annual bond at a 6% yield (price 100):

Year 1: PV 5.660, weight 0.0566, t × w = 0.0566
Year 2: PV 5.340, weight 0.0534, t × w = 0.1068
Year 3: PV 89.000, weight 0.8900, t × w = 2.6700

MacDur = **2.83 years**. A 3-year zero would have MacDur = 3.00.

cards.title: Duration properties
cards.body:
- **Zero-coupon bond:** MacDur = maturity.
- **Coupon bond:** MacDur < maturity (coupons pull the average earlier).
- Higher coupon → lower duration; higher yield → lower duration.
- **Perpetuity:** MacDur = (1 + r)/r. At 5%: 21 years.

MacDur is both a measure of the **weighted-average time to receive cash** and the **investment horizon** at which reinvestment and price risk offset.

cards.title: Duration gap
where: price risk dominates: investor is hurt by rising rates
reinvestment risk dominates: investor is hurt by falling rates
approximately immunized for a one-off parallel shift

cards.title: Duration gap in action
cards.body:
The 5-year 6% bond at 6% has MacDur = **4.47**.

- Horizon 2 years: gap = +2.47 → price risk dominates. Rates up 100 bp → realized return 4.78% (< 6%); rates down to 5% → 7.25%.
- Horizon 5 years: gap = −0.53 → reinvestment risk dominates. Rates up → 6.11%; rates down → 5.89%.

cards.title: ACCA vs CFA
cards.body: AFM used duration to compare bond risk. CFA tests the **horizon logic**: match MacDur to your horizon to neutralize a one-time rate shift. Learn the sign of the gap and which risk dominates; questions rarely require a full duration calculation without the table.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a source of return for a fixed-rate bond investor?
options: Capital gain or loss on sale before maturity
Changes in the issuer's dividend policy
questions.explanation: The three sources are coupons, reinvestment income and capital gains/losses. Dividend policy affects shareholders, not the bond's cash flows directly.

questions.stem: An investor buys a 5-year 6% annual bond at par. Yields immediately rise to 7% and stay there. If she holds to maturity, her annualized realized return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Coupons reinvested at 7% grow to 6 × [(1.07^{5} − 1)/0.07] = 34.50. Total = 134.50; return = 1.3450^{1/5} − 1 = 6.11%. 6.00% ignores the higher reinvestment rate; 5.89% is the result if rates had fallen to 5%.

questions.stem: For the same bond and rate rise (6% par bond, yields to 7%), if the investor sells after 2 years, her annualized return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Coupons with reinvestment = 6 + 6 × 1.07 = 12.42. Sale price (3 years at 7%) = 97.38. Total 109.80 → 1.0980^{1/2} − 1 = 4.78%. The short horizon means the price loss outweighs higher reinvestment income; 6.11% is the hold-to-maturity result.

questions.stem: An investor bought a 5-year 6% annual bond at 95.90 (YTM 7%). Two years later she sells at 98.50. The bond's carrying value at a 7% yield is 97.38. Her capital gain is closest to:
questions.explanation: Capital gain = sale price − carrying value = 98.50 − 97.38 = 1.12. 2.60 measures against purchase price, treating discount amortization (1.48) as a capital gain; 1.48 is the amortization itself, which is interest income.

questions.stem: A 3-year 6% annual bond yields 6%. Its Macaulay duration is closest to:
questions.explanation: Weights: 0.0566, 0.0534, 0.8900. MacDur = 1 × 0.0566 + 2 × 0.0534 + 3 × 0.8900 = 2.83. 3.00 is the maturity (true only for a zero); 2.67 counts only the final cash flow's contribution.

questions.stem: A bond has a Macaulay duration of 8 years. An investor's horizon is 6 years. Which risk dominates?
options: Reinvestment risk, so falling rates hurt.
Market price risk, so rising rates hurt.
Neither, because the bond is immunized.
questions.explanation: Duration gap = 8 − 6 = +2 > 0: the investor will sell a bond with considerable remaining duration, so price risk dominates and rising rates reduce the realized return.

questions.stem: The Macaulay duration of a 7-year zero-coupon bond is:
questions.explanation: A zero has a single cash flow at maturity, so all weight is at year 7. Coupon bonds have MacDur below maturity.

questions.stem: The Macaulay duration of a perpetuity yielding 5% is closest to:
questions.explanation: MacDur = (1 + r)/r = 1.05/0.05 = 21. 20 is 1/r (modified-duration-style result); duration is finite because distant cash flows have tiny present values.

questions.stem: An investor with a 5-year horizon buys a 5-year 6% annual bond at par (MacDur 4.47). Yields fall immediately to 5% and stay there. Her realized annual return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Holding to maturity, coupons are reinvested at 5%: 6 × [(1.05^{5} − 1)/0.05] = 33.15; total 133.15 → 5.89%. The negative duration gap (4.47 − 5) means reinvestment risk dominates, so falling rates hurt. 7.25% is the 2-year-horizon result.

questions.stem: All else equal, which change increases a coupon bond's Macaulay duration?
questions.explanation: A lower coupon shifts relative value to the final principal payment, lengthening the weighted-average time. Higher coupons and higher yields both shorten duration.

questions.stem: An investor buys a 4-year 5% annual bond at par and holds to maturity. Yields fall immediately to 4% and stay there. Her realized return is closest to:
questions.explanation: Coupons reinvested at 4%: 5 × [(1.04^{4} − 1)/0.04] = 21.23; total 121.23 → 1.2123^{1/4} − 1 = 4.93%. 5.00% assumes reinvestment at the original YTM; 7.78% is the return from selling after one year at the higher price.

questions.stem: A pension fund must pay a fixed amount in 4.5 years and holds a bond with a Macaulay duration of 4.5 years. Following a one-time parallel rise in yields, the fund's realized return over 4.5 years will most likely be:
options: approximately equal to the original yield.
well below the original yield because prices fall.
well above the original yield because reinvestment income rises.
questions.explanation: With a zero duration gap, the price loss and the higher reinvestment income roughly offset, so the realized horizon return stays close to the original YTM. That is the logic of immunization against a single parallel shift.

flashcards.back: Coupons, reinvestment income on coupons, capital gain/loss on sale.
MacDur = Σ t × PV(CF_{t})/Price: weighted-average time to cash flows.
MacDur − investment horizon. > 0: price risk dominates. < 0: reinvestment risk dominates.
Help the investor: reinvestment gains outweigh price losses.
Zero: = maturity. Perpetuity: (1 + r)/r.
Sale price − carrying value (amortized cost at purchase YTM), not purchase price.
Higher coupon → lower duration. Higher yield → lower duration. Longer maturity → usually higher.
